questions.stem: A client is transferred from the emergency department to an inpatient unit after receiving a new IV antibiotic and being identified as high fall risk. What should the handoff include?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Provide the new room number without additional clinical detail because the receiving nurse can locate the remaining information in the electronic record.","B":"Communicate current clinical status, treatment given, pending information, fall risk and precautions, and allow the receiving nurse to clarify questions.","C":"Provide billing, insurance, and transport details while omitting most clinical information because the chart already contains the medical record.","D":"Skip direct handoff communication because transferring responsibility through the electronic chart alone is sufficient without acknowledgment by the receiver."}}
questions.rationale: A safe handoff transfers the information, responsibility, and accountability needed for the receiving team to continue care. Option B is correct because it communicates current status, treatment, pending information, fall risk and precautions, and supports clarification. Option A supplies only a location. Option C omits clinically essential information. Option D incorrectly assumes electronic documentation alone replaces acknowledged handoff communication.
questions.source_detail: AHRQ defines handoff as transfer of information, authority, and responsibility during transitions in care; proper handoff requires clear verbal communication, acknowledgment by the receiver, and an opportunity to clarify and confirm.

qc.qc_note: Strict final audit: max/min option-character ratio <=1.15; keyed option within 10% of distractor mean; keyed option is neither shortest nor longest; distractors manually reviewed for clinical plausibility, grammatical parallelism, and answer-cue leakage.
